thread: Follow a waterway from canal locks to working boats and out into a busy maritime port. The swarm encounters the machinery that moves vessels, the vessels themselves, and the curious instruments and cargoes they carry.

candidates.name: London Canal Museum
candidates.why: Narrowboats, lock machinery, a squat Bantam tug, a Bolinder engine, and even the ice wells of a former warehouse give the swarm a mechanical canal-side beginning.

candidates.name: National Historic Ships UK
candidates.why: A fleet of historic tugs, barges, fishing boats and other vessels offers hull shapes, propulsion systems, construction details and restoration crafts to inhabit.

candidates.name: Maritime Museum of Barcelona
candidates.why: At the port, ship models, anchors, binnacles, navigational instruments and a sailing schooner turn the swarm into a lively collection of seafaring objects.

candidates.name: Canal & River Trust
candidates.why: Canal routes, aqueducts, locks, working boats and the National Waterways Museum's dredgers and icebreakers provide another route from inland engineering toward the sea.

candidates.name: New Zealand Maritime Museum
candidates.why: Heritage boats, ship models, charts, maritime crafts and the Percy Vos boat shed give the swarm vessels to build and a harbour to explore.

candidates.name: Maritime Museum Tasmania
candidates.why: Tasmanian ships, harbour history, nautical objects and maritime records offer island-flavoured vessels and portside creatures.

candidates.name: Australian National Maritime Museum
candidates.why: Historic vessels, boats, nautical instruments and a large collection ranging from rocket boats to tiny maritime objects offer plenty of shapes for the swarm.

candidates.name: Dubrovnik Museums
candidates.why: The maritime collections and shipwrights' tools evoke a historic harbour filled with wooden ships, models and the implements that made them.
